overview.title: Video tensors and the Dense layer as a tensor function
overview.chapter: 2 The mathematical building blocks of neural networks
overview.section: 2.3 The gears of neural networks: Tensor operations
overview.main_topic: Finishing the data-tensor catalogue (channels-first image shapes, rank-5 video tensors and their memory cost) and opening section 2.3: every transformation a network learns is a composition of a few tensor operations, exemplified by `output = relu(matmul(input, W) + b)` for a Dense layer.
overview.central_idea: Data can be as large as a rank-5 video tensor, yet what a network does to it reduces to a handful of tensor operations; a `Dense(512, activation="relu")` layer is just the function `relu(matmul(input, W) + b)` with its own matrix `W` and vector `b`.
overview.importance: This page is the hinge of the chapter: it closes the "what is the data" half and opens the "what do layers do to it" half. The Dense-layer formula introduced here is unpacked over the next ten pages (tensor product, addition with broadcasting, relu) and later interpreted geometrically (p.59-62) and differentiated (p.63 onward).
learning_objectives: Convert the image-batch examples between channels-last and channels-first layouts.
Build the rank-5 shape of a batch of video clips and compute its element count and memory footprint in float32.
State the claim that all learned transformations reduce to a handful of tensor operations, and the analogy with binary logic gates.
Read `keras.layers.Dense(512, activation="relu")` as the function `output = relu(matmul(input, W) + b)` and identify `W` and `b` as the layer's attributes.
prerequisites: The first MNIST model built from Dense layers (p.43)

summary:
**Channels-first examples.** In the channels-first convention, the two image batches of p.51 become `(128, 1, 256, 256)` and `(128, 3, 256, 256)`. Keras supports both formats.

**Video data.** Video is one of the few real-world data types that needs rank-5 tensors. A video is a sequence of frames and each frame is a color image. A frame is a rank-3 tensor `(height, width, color_depth)`, a sequence of frames is rank 4 `(frames, height, width, color_depth)`, and a batch of videos is rank 5 `(samples, frames, height, width, color_depth)`. Figure 2.4, placed alongside, draws the rank-4 image tensor with axes Color channels, Height, Width and Samples. Worked example: a 60-second 144 × 256 YouTube clip sampled at 4 frames per second has 240 frames; a batch of four such clips is `(4, 240, 144, 256, 3)`, a total of 106,168,320 values. In `float32` (32 bits per value) that is 425 MB. Real videos are far lighter because they are not stored as `float32` and are heavily compressed (e.g. MPEG).

**2.3 The gears of neural networks: Tensor operations.** Just as any computer program reduces to a small set of binary operations on binary inputs (`AND`, `OR`, `NOR`, …), every transformation learned by a deep neural network reduces to a handful of *tensor operations* (or *tensor functions*) on numeric tensors, such as adding or multiplying tensors. The first example stacked `Dense` layers; a Keras layer instance looks like `keras.layers.Dense(512, activation="relu")`. Such a layer is a function from a matrix to a new matrix, a new representation of the input. Specifically, with `W` a matrix and `b` a vector that are both attributes of the layer:

```
output = relu(matmul(input, W) + b)
```

The next page unpacks this into three tensor operations (a tensor product `matmul`, an addition, and `relu(x) = max(x, 0)`) and notes that the book will express linear algebra as NumPy snippets rather than mathematical notation.

paragraphs.what_it_says: Video is one of the few real-world data types needing rank-5 tensors. A video is a sequence of frames, each a color image; a frame is a rank-3 `(height, width, color_depth)` tensor.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The by-now familiar nesting: image (rank 3) inside a sequence (rank 4) inside a batch (rank 5). The authors emphasise "one of the few" because, as p.47 said, you will generally manipulate ranks 0 to 4.

paragraphs.what_it_says: A sequence of frames is a rank-4 tensor `(frames, height, width, color_depth)`, so a batch of videos is a rank-5 tensor `(samples, frames, height, width, color_depth)`.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Each added level of structure adds an axis in front. Note the naming: inside one video the frame axis comes first; in the batch it becomes axis 1, exactly like the time axis of sequence data.

paragraphs.excerpt: For instance, a 60-second, 144 × 256 YouTube video clip sampled at 4 frames
paragraphs.what_it_says: A 60-second 144 × 256 clip at 4 fps has 240 frames. Four such clips form `(4, 240, 144, 256, 3)`: 106,168,320 values. As `float32` (32 bits each) that is 425 MB. Real videos are much lighter because they are not stored in `float32` and are compressed by large factors (e.g. MPEG).
paragraphs.what_it_means: The element count is the product of the shape: 4 × 240 × 144 × 256 × 3 = 106,168,320. At 4 bytes per value that is 424,673,280 bytes ≈ 425 MB (decimal megabytes). Only four short, low-resolution clips already approach half a gigabyte once decoded to float tensors, which is why video models work on small batches, few frames, and reduced resolution.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: First time the book connects shape to memory. The dtype matters as much as the shape: `uint8` pixels would take a quarter of the space; compressed video on disk takes far less again. This cost drives many practical design choices in later chapters (resizing images, batch sizes).
paragraphs.technical_idea: Memory = (product of shape) × (bytes per element). `float32` = 4 bytes, `float16` = 2, `uint8` = 1. Beyond the book: 424,673,280 bytes is 405 MiB if you count in binary mebibytes; the book uses decimal MB.

terminology.meaning: Sampling rate of the video in time; 4 fps × 60 s = 240 frames.
A family of lossy video compression formats; mentioned as the reason real video files are far smaller than their decoded float tensors.

p.43: MNIST pixels converted from `uint8` to `float32` before training.

paragraphs.excerpt: Just like any computer program can be ultimately reduced to a small set
paragraphs.what_it_says: As any program reduces to a few binary operations on bits (`AND`, `OR`, `NOR`, …), every transformation learned by a deep network reduces to a handful of *tensor operations* (tensor functions) on numeric tensors: adding tensors, multiplying tensors, and so on.
paragraphs.what_it_means: This is the thesis of section 2.3. However elaborate a model looks, it is a composition of a small vocabulary of primitives. Learn the primitives and you can read any architecture.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It reframes a neural network from a mysterious black box into a chain of simple, inspectable operations, which is also what makes automatic differentiation (section 2.4) possible: differentiate each primitive, chain the results.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book: the analogy is apt in a stronger sense. Logic gates are *functionally complete* for boolean functions; a sufficiently wide chain of affine maps and relu is a universal approximator for continuous functions, so a small set of tensor primitives suffices in principle as well.

terminology.meaning: A function that takes one or more tensors and returns a tensor, e.g. addition, product, relu.

connections: p.82: chapter summary: "Deep learning models consist of chains of simple tensor operations, parameterized by weights".

paragraphs.excerpt: In our initial example, we were building our model by stacking Dense layers
paragraphs.what_it_says: The initial example stacked `Dense` layers. A Keras layer instance looks like `keras.layers.Dense(512, activation="relu")`.
paragraphs.what_it_means: This is the first hidden layer of the MNIST model from p.43: 512 output units with the relu activation. The page is about to tell you what this object computes.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Grounds the abstract claim about tensor operations in the one concrete model the reader has already trained.
paragraphs.technical_idea: `512` is the number of output units (columns of `W`); `activation="relu"` selects the nonlinearity applied after the affine part.

terminology.meaning: A fully connected layer: every output unit depends on every input feature through the weight matrix `W`.

connections: p.43: the model `Sequential([Dense(512, activation="relu"), Dense(10, activation="softmax")])`.

paragraphs.excerpt: This layer can be interpreted as a function, which takes as input a matrix
paragraphs.what_it_says: The layer is a function from a matrix to another matrix, a new *representation* of the input. Specifically, with `W` a matrix and `b` a vector that are attributes of the layer: `output = relu(matmul(input, W) + b)`.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The input matrix is a batch of samples `(samples, input_features)`; `matmul` with `W` of shape `(input_features, 512)` produces `(samples, 512)`; the vector `b` of length 512 is added to every row; relu zeroes the negatives. The output is again a matrix, so another Dense layer can follow. `W` and `b` are the *weights*: they are stored in the layer and are what training adjusts.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This single line is the template for most of deep learning: an affine map (`matmul` + `b`) followed by a nonlinearity. Pages 53-58 explain each operation, p.59-62 interpret them geometrically, and p.63-75 show how `W` and `b` are learned.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Three operations, evaluated inside out: tensor product, then addition (which needs broadcasting because `b` is a vector and the product is a matrix, p.54), then element-wise relu (p.53).

terminology.meaning: The transformed version of the data a layer outputs; the book's view of layers as learning useful representations (chapter 1).
The layer's weight matrix and bias vector, attributes of the layer object.

connections: p.53: the three operations unpacked; relu(x) = max(x, 0).
p.59: geometric interpretation of these operations.

concepts.name: Video data tensor
concepts.definition: A rank-5 tensor `(samples, frames, height, width, color_depth)`: a batch of videos, each a sequence of color-image frames.
concepts.intuition: A flip-book of photos is a video; a shelf of flip-books is a batch.
concepts.technical: frame `(height, width, color_depth)` → video `(frames, height, width, color_depth)` → batch, rank 5. Element count is the product of the shape; memory = count × bytes per element.
concepts.significance: The largest-rank data you will routinely see, and a reminder that decoded tensors are enormous: four short clips already cost 425 MB in float32.
concepts.misconception: That a video file of a few MB becomes a tensor of a few MB. Decoding to float32 pixels expands it by orders of magnitude because compression is undone and each value takes 4 bytes.

concepts.name: Tensor operation
concepts.definition: A function applied to numeric tensors that returns a tensor (addition, product, relu, …); the book's claim is that all transformations learned by deep networks reduce to a handful of these.
concepts.intuition: Like logic gates for programs: a tiny instruction set that composes into anything.
concepts.technical: A layer is a tensor function parameterized by weight tensors; a model is a chain of such functions. Because each primitive is simple and differentiable, the chain can be trained by gradient descent (section 2.4).
concepts.significance: Makes architectures readable and differentiable; the rest of section 2.3 catalogues the primitives (element-wise ops, broadcasting, tensor product, reshaping).
concepts.example: `output = relu(matmul(input, W) + b)` uses exactly three: `matmul`, `+`, `relu`.
concepts.misconception: That deep networks rely on exotic mathematics. The operations are elementary; depth and learned weights, not complicated primitives, give them power.

concepts.name: Dense layer as a function
concepts.definition: A Keras `Dense` layer computes `output = relu(matmul(input, W) + b)` (with relu as the chosen activation), where `W` is a weight matrix and `b` a bias vector stored as attributes of the layer.
concepts.intuition: Each of the 512 output units takes a weighted sum of all input features, adds its own offset, and reports it only if positive.
concepts.technical: Input `(samples, n_in)`, `W` `(n_in, units)`, `b` `(units,)`, output `(samples, units)`. The matmul mixes features linearly, the bias shifts, relu introduces nonlinearity. For the first MNIST layer n_in = 784, units = 512, so W has 401,408 entries and b 512 (my count; the book gives the formula, not the numbers).
concepts.significance: The prototypical layer; the formula generalizes (with different products) to convolutions, recurrent cells and attention.
concepts.example: `keras.layers.Dense(512, activation="relu")` on a `(128, 784)` batch returns a `(128, 512)` matrix.
concepts.misconception: That `W` and `b` are inputs to the layer. They are attributes owned by the layer; only `input` is passed in. Training changes `W` and `b`, not the formula.

math.title: The Dense layer function

variables.meaning: a matrix of shape (samples, n_in): one row per sample
the layer's weight matrix, shape (n_in, units); an attribute of the layer
the layer's bias vector, shape (units,); an attribute of the layer
the new representation, a matrix of shape (samples, units)

math.operations: Inside out: a tensor product `matmul(input, W)`, then an addition of the vector `b` to every row of the result (broadcasting, p.54), then the element-wise `relu`.
math.purpose: Defines what a `Dense(units, activation="relu")` layer computes; it is the building block the first MNIST model stacked twice.
math.interpretation: An affine transformation of the input features (a learned linear mixing plus a shift), followed by a nonlinearity so that stacked layers do not collapse into a single linear map.
math.intuition: Each output unit is a weighted vote over all input features, offset by a bias, and clipped at zero.
math.numerical_example:
Take a batch of 2 samples with 3 features and a layer with 2 units (small numbers for illustration; not from the book):

$$\text{input} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix},\quad W = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 2 \\ 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix},\quad b = (0.5,\; -3)$$

`matmul(input, W)` = [[1·1+0·0+2·1, 1·(−1)+0·2+2·1], [0+0+1, 0+2+1]] = [[3, 1], [1, 3]]. Adding b to each row: [[3.5, −2], [1.5, 0]]. relu: [[3.5, 0], [1.5, 0]]. Output shape (2, 2) = (samples, units).

math.title: Element count and memory of the video batch
math.source_text: a tensor of shape (4, 240, 144, 256, 3). That’s a total of 106,168,320 values! If the dtype of the tensor was float32, then each value would be stored in 32 bits, so the tensor would represent 425 MB.

variables.meaning: number of scalar values in the tensor, the product of its shape
size of one float32 value (32 bits)

math.operations: Multiply the axis lengths to count elements; multiply by bytes per element for memory.
math.purpose: Shows how quickly realistic data tensors become large and why dtype and compression matter.
math.interpretation: Four short low-resolution clips decoded to float32 occupy about 425 MB; the same clips on disk as MPEG are a tiny fraction of that.
math.intuition: Every extra axis multiplies the size; five axes multiply fast.
math.numerical_example: 4 × 240 = 960; × 144 = 138,240; × 256 = 35,389,440; × 3 = 106,168,320 values. × 4 bytes = 424,673,280 bytes ≈ 425 MB (decimal). As `uint8` it would be 106 MB; as `float16`, 212 MB. (The uint8/float16 figures are mine.)

code.title: A Keras Dense layer instance
code.what_it_does: Creates a fully connected layer with 512 output units and the relu activation, the first layer of the MNIST model on p.43.

line_explanations.explanation: `512` is the number of units (the width of the output matrix and the number of columns of `W`); `activation="relu"` chooses the nonlinearity applied after `matmul(input, W) + b`. `W` and `b` are created when the layer first sees its input shape.

code.inputs_outputs: Called on a matrix `(samples, n_in)`, it returns a matrix `(samples, 512)`.
code.algorithm: Instantiation only; the computation is the formula in the next snippet.
code.theory_link: A layer is a tensor function with its own weight tensors `W` and `b`.

parameters.name: activation="relu"
parameters.role: element-wise nonlinearity applied to the affine output

pitfalls: Omitting `activation` gives a purely linear layer; stacking several of those is equivalent to a single linear layer (discussed on p.62).

code.title: What the Dense layer computes
code.what_it_does: Pseudocode for the layer's forward computation: tensor product with `W`, add `b`, apply relu.

line_explanations.explanation: Evaluated inside out: `matmul(input, W)` mixes the input features linearly into 512 new ones per sample; `+ b` adds the bias vector to every row (broadcasting); `relu` replaces negatives by 0. `W` is a matrix and `b` a vector, both attributes of the layer, not arguments.

code.algorithm: Three tensor operations: tensor product, element-wise addition with broadcasting, element-wise relu (each detailed on p.53-58).
code.theory_link: An affine transformation followed by a nonlinearity; the geometric reading is given on p.59-62.
pitfalls: The order of `matmul(input, W)` matters: with `input` as `(samples, n_in)` the weights must be `(n_in, units)`; `matmul(W, input)` would fail or mean something else.
code.illustrative_code:
import numpy as np

def relu(x):
    return np.maximum(x, 0.)

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
x = rng.random((128, 784)).astype("float32")   # a batch of 128 flattened MNIST images
W = rng.standard_normal((784, 512)).astype("float32") * 0.05
b = np.zeros((512,), dtype="float32")

output = relu(np.matmul(x, W) + b)
print(output.shape)         # (128, 512)
print((output >= 0).all())  # True: relu never outputs negatives

deeper.title: Why a 425 MB tensor comes from a tiny video file
deeper.body:
The book's clip is 60 s at 144 × 256, 4 fps. Where do the bytes go?

- Decoded pixels per frame: 144 × 256 × 3 = 110,592 values.
- Per clip: × 240 frames = 26,542,080 values.
- Per batch of 4: 106,168,320 values (the number on the page).
- As float32: × 4 bytes = 424,673,280 bytes ≈ 425 MB.

Two things inflate the tensor relative to the file on disk. First, dtype: pixels are naturally `uint8` (1 byte), so float32 quadruples the size. Second, compression: an MPEG-style codec stores only differences between neighbouring frames and discards imperceptible detail, routinely shrinking data by 50–100×. A few megabytes of MP4 therefore become hundreds of megabytes of float tensor once decoded. This is why video pipelines decode lazily, batch by batch, rather than loading a dataset into memory. (The decomposition and compression ratios are added here; the book gives only the final figures.)

deeper.title: Reading the Dense formula one operation at a time
deeper.body:
Take the first MNIST layer, `Dense(512, activation="relu")`, fed a batch of 128 flattened images.

1. **`input`** has shape `(128, 784)`: 128 samples, 784 pixel features.
2. **`matmul(input, W)`** with `W` of shape `(784, 512)` gives `(128, 512)`. Each of the 512 columns of `W` is a set of 784 weights, one per pixel; each output entry is a weighted sum of all pixels of one image.
3. **`+ b`** adds the 512-vector `b` to every one of the 128 rows (broadcasting, p.54). Shape stays `(128, 512)`.
4. **`relu(...)`** replaces each negative entry by 0, independently of all other entries (element-wise, p.53).
5. **`output`** is `(128, 512)`: a new 512-feature representation of each image, ready for the next layer `Dense(10, activation="softmax")`.

The parameter count of this layer is 784 × 512 + 512 = 401,920 (the arithmetic is mine; the book introduces the formula only).

deeper.title: Logic gates and tensor operations
deeper.body: The authors compare tensor operations to the binary gates (`AND`, `OR`, `NOR`) that every program bottoms out in. Push the analogy one step: a CPU does not care whether it is running a spreadsheet or a game; it only executes gate-level instructions, and the *program* (the arrangement of instructions) is what differs. Likewise a deep learning framework only executes tensor products, additions and element-wise functions; the *model* is the arrangement of those operations, and the *weights* `W` and `b` are the data that arrangement operates with. Section 2.3 is the instruction-set manual; section 2.4 explains how the weights get written.

misconceptions.claim: Video tensors are rank 4 because a video is just a set of images.
misconceptions.correction: A single video is rank 4 `(frames, height, width, color_depth)`; a *batch* of videos adds the samples axis and is rank 5.

misconceptions.claim: A 425 MB tensor means the video files take 425 MB on disk.
misconceptions.correction: 425 MB is the decoded float32 tensor. Real videos are stored compressed (e.g. MPEG) and not as float32, so the files are far smaller.

misconceptions.claim: `W` and `b` are passed to the Dense layer when you call it.
misconceptions.correction: They are attributes of the layer object; the layer is called with `input` only. Training updates `W` and `b`.

misconceptions.claim: Neural networks require advanced mathematics beyond ordinary tensor arithmetic.
misconceptions.correction: The page's point is the opposite: all learned transformations reduce to a handful of tensor operations such as addition and multiplication (plus simple element-wise functions).

takeaways: Channels-first versions of the image batches are `(128, 1, 256, 256)` and `(128, 3, 256, 256)`; Keras supports both layouts.
Video is rank 5: frame `(height, width, color_depth)` → clip `(frames, …)` → batch `(samples, frames, height, width, color_depth)`.
Four 60-second 144 × 256 clips at 4 fps form `(4, 240, 144, 256, 3)`: 106,168,320 values, 425 MB in float32; real videos are smaller because of dtype and compression.
All transformations learned by deep networks reduce to a handful of tensor operations, as programs reduce to logic gates.
A `Dense(512, activation="relu")` layer computes `output = relu(matmul(input, W) + b)`, with `W` (matrix) and `b` (vector) stored as attributes of the layer.

questions.question: Verify the book's count: how many values are in a tensor of shape `(4, 240, 144, 256, 3)`, and how many bytes does it occupy as float32?
questions.explanation: The element count is the product of all axis lengths, and float32 stores each value in 32 bits = 4 bytes, matching the 425 MB stated on the page.

questions.question: In the channels-first convention, how is the batch of 128 color 256 × 256 images stored?
questions.explanation: Channels-first puts color depth right after the batch axis. `(128, 256, 256, 3)` is channels-last; `(3, 128, 256, 256)` puts channels before samples, which no convention does; `(128, 256, 3, 256)` places channels between height and width.

questions.question: Why are real-world video files much lighter than the 425 MB tensor computed on the page?
questions.answer: Because they are not stored as float32 values and they are compressed by a large factor (for example with MPEG).
questions.explanation: The page gives both reasons: dtype (float32 uses 4 bytes per value, far more than needed for pixel data) and compression (codecs such as MPEG shrink the data substantially).

questions.question: What analogy do the authors use to introduce tensor operations, and what claim does it support?
questions.answer: Just as any computer program reduces to a small set of binary operations on binary inputs (AND, OR, NOR, …), all transformations learned by deep neural networks reduce to a handful of tensor operations (adding, multiplying tensors, and so on) applied to numeric tensors.
questions.explanation: The analogy frames section 2.3: a deep network, however complex, is composed from a few simple primitives, which the section then catalogues.

questions.question: In `output = relu(matmul(input, W) + b)`, what are `W` and `b`?
options: Two extra input tensors supplied with each batch
A matrix and a vector that are attributes of the Dense layer
Hyperparameters chosen by the user, like the number of units
The output shape and the batch size
questions.answer: A matrix and a vector that are attributes of the Dense layer
questions.explanation: The page says `W` is a matrix and `b` a vector, both attributes of the layer. They are not inputs (only `input` is passed in), not hyperparameters (they are learned, whereas 512 units is a hyperparameter), and not shapes.

questions.question: If `input` has shape `(128, 784)` and the layer is `Dense(512, activation="relu")`, what are the shapes of `W`, `b` and `output`?
questions.explanation: `matmul(input, W)` requires W's first axis to match the 784 input features and its second axis to be the 512 units; `b` has one entry per unit and is added to every row; the output keeps the 128 samples and has 512 features. (Shapes are derived from the formula; the page states the formula but not these specific numbers.)

questions.question: Can you list the three tensor operations hidden in `relu(matmul(input, W) + b)`, in the order they are executed, and say which upcoming subsection explains each?
questions.answer: 1. Tensor product `matmul(input, W)` (2.3.3, p.56); 2. addition of the vector `b` to the matrix, which relies on broadcasting (2.3.1 element-wise ops p.53 and 2.3.2 broadcasting p.54); 3. element-wise `relu` (2.3.1, p.53).
questions.explanation: The next page lists exactly these three operations; the chapter outline shows where each is treated. If you could not name them, re-read the last paragraph of this page and p.53.
